blocks.title: Honors transfer task — same numbers, higher bar
blocks.markdown: You get the **same scenario and the same data** as CPA: 2026-XJ at 1.2×10⁸ km, 8,500 m/s at 15° toward Earth. The calculation isn't harder. What's raised is the **demand**: state your assumptions and their limits, defend the model in writing, and locate this task in the year's arc. The bar moves, not the numbers.

## Part B — Justify (the honors raise)

After the Part-A calculation (position, velocity components, uncertainty window, position-vs-time graph), you owe three things in writing:

- **State every assumption** your prediction rests on — you have at least four (constant velocity, negligible force over this leg, point particle, motion confined to a plane) — and for **each**, the physical condition under which it would break.
- **Defend the constant-velocity model** against the classmate who says *'acceleration is negligible, so it's a perfectly straight line we can pinpoint exactly.'* Their arithmetic is fine; the reasoning is not. Find the flaw.
- **Translate the math into physics:** what the 15° angle means for whether it hits us, and why the uncertainty window *grows* over six months instead of staying fixed.

blocks.frame: Assumption: ___. It would break when ___.  (Repeat for each of your four.)
blocks.prompt: STATE EVERY ASSUMPTION AND WHEN IT BREAKS: List every assumption your six-month prediction rests on (at least four). For EACH one, pair it with the specific physical condition under which it would fail. A bare list of assumptions without breaking conditions caps your Reasoning at 3.

blocks.frame: The classmate's MODEL error is ___. Their DATA error is ___. These are different because a model error comes from ___ while a data error comes from ___.
blocks.prompt: REBUTTAL — model error vs data error: Your classmate's numbers are right but their claim ('a perfectly straight line we can pinpoint exactly') is wrong for TWO separate reasons. Name both: the model error (the constant-velocity assumption) AND the data error (the ± measurement uncertainties). Explain why missing either one is an incomplete rebuttal.
